description: The Druk (Thunder Dragon) is Bhutan's national symbol, giving the country its name Druk Yul ('Land of the Thunder Dragon'). The 12th-century Tibetan master Tsangpa Gyare heard thunder thrice while founding Ralung Monastery and named his Drukpa Kagyu lineage after it; the dragon later became Bhutan's emblem. The Druk commands storms — its roar is thunder, its serpentine body lightning.
source: Drukpa Kagyu tradition, Bhutanese national history, Pema Lingpa's terma revelations

description: The Bolotnik ('Swamp Spirit') is a malevolent spirit of Belarusian and western Russian folklore, the name from 'boloto,' Slavic for swamp. Unlike the Vodyanoy of deep waters, he haunts shallow, unstable bogs and marshes. Said to be the soul of a drowned person or one cursed to guard the wetlands, he seizes travelers' ankles from beneath and drags them into the peat, bodies never found.
source: Belarusian folklore — Bolotnik swamp spirit documented in Belarusian oral tradition.

description: Aluxes are small, elf-like trickster spirits of the Yucatec Maya. They haunt ruins, cenotes, forests, and cornfields, hiding tools, leading travelers astray, and stealing food. Given corn, honey, or balché, they become protective guardians; farmers build small stone 'kahtal alux' houses at field corners to guard crops. An alux lives seven years unless regularly 'fed.'
source: Mesoamerican mythology, Popol Vuh & Florentine Codex

description: Santa Muerte ('Holy Death') is a folk saint and personification of death venerated in Mexico, blending the Aztec death goddess Mictēcacihuātl with the Spanish Grim Reaper. Her robe colors mark the request — white for purification, red for love, gold for money, black for protection, green for justice. Despite the Church's rejection, her cult grew in the early 2000s, among the marginalized.
source: Mexican folk religion — Santa Muerte is the folk saint of death documented in contemporary Mexican tradition.

description: Bon Bibi (Bonobibi), 'Lady of the Forest,' is the guardian goddess of the Sundarbans mangrove delta between Bangladesh and India, worshipped by Hindu and Muslim honey collectors, woodcutters, and fishermen. Legend holds that Allah sent her to protect the faithful from Dakshin Ray, the demon king who demanded sacrifices; she defeated him and won a truce, guarding all who enter with respect.
source: Bangladesh mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

description: Taleju Bhawani is a tantric form of Durga and royal tutelary goddess of the Malla kings. Legend says King Jayaprakash Malla played dice nightly with her; when his daughter discovered them, the goddess vanished, but commanded in a dream that he worship a Shakya virgin girl as her living embodiment — founding the Kumari tradition. Her Kathmandu Durbar Square temple was built in 1564.
source: Taleju Bhawani temple history, Malla dynasty chronicles, Nepali Newar traditions

description: Singbonga is the supreme creator god of the Munda; his name means 'Sun God.' In the creation myth he set a cosmic egg afloat on a primordial sea, from which hatched Horo the tortoise and Karakom the crab. The tortoise brought earth up on its back, and when the land proved too soft, a great spider's web solidified it. He then made the first humans, sun, moon, and stars.
source: Munda oral traditions, Sarna religion, tribal folklore of Jharkhand
